name: Jamal Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Jamal. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not connected to any AI company, employer, union or government. What you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. Okay to go ahead?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, go ahead. I told Ines I was doing a research interview and she said, don't make us sound boring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me what a normal working day looks like for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at an open-pit copper mine, the big one with the bucket you could park two cars in. I'm the lead operator on B crew, so I set the dig plan with the shift supervisor and train the newer operators. Twelve-hour shifts, four on, four off. The best part is when you've got six haul trucks lined up and you're loading each one in three passes, no waiting, like a dance. The worst part is the night shift in winter, when the cab heater is broken and you're watching the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but nicely. A lot of the guys have been nervous about the autonomous trucks they keep talking about, and if it all fizzles out they'll relax. I'd probably post a meme in the crew group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep climbing. I'm already lead on my crew at twenty-seven, so the next step is shift supervisor in a few years. If AI turns out to be hype, I'm just a young guy with a good job and a long road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Put more into the shares account, keep paying down the car, maybe do the supervisor course the company offers. Ines and I talked about buying a place in about two years, and that stays on track.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for, at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly translating. We've got operators from three countries on site, and I'll use a chatbot to turn the safety notes into simple Spanish and Tagalog so everybody gets them. Sometimes I ask it to explain a spec in the shovel manual. It's handy, nothing magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss, if the big change never came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. Part of me wanted to see what a fully automated pit looks like. But I wouldn't miss the worry on the older guys' faces.

S0.say: He'd tell the crew he'd called it, kindly, because many of them are nervous about autonomous trucks. He'd probably post a meme in the crew group chat.
S0.think: Privately he sees a long, steady career ahead: lead operator at 27, with shift supervisor as the next step in a few years.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, puts more into his share account and keeps paying down the car. Takes the company's supervisor course and keeps the plan to buy a place with Ines in about two years.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be hype, I'm just a young guy with a good job and a long road.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal sees his career as a ladder he is climbing fast, and a flop simply leaves the ladder in place. He uses AI in a modest, practical way to translate safety notes for a multilingual crew. His concern is mostly for older workers, not himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a proper plan for the people who lose seats. The trucks will go autonomous first, they already have at some mines, so drivers need a guaranteed path into other jobs, paid for by the company. I'd say the union should be at the table from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the shovel lasts longer than the trucks. Loading is harder to automate because the face keeps changing. But the trucks going means half my crew mates go, and those are my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to train on the remote operating station as soon as the mine sets one up, and push to get two of my younger operators in with me. I'd start learning the autonomous haulage software properly, not just poking at it. And I'd put aside an extra few hundred a month, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd be fine, probably, but I'd feel weird being fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go for one of the remote control room jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, but only once I'd seen it work on our site. I'm not going to be the first one in the chair when the bugs are still in it. Once two or three people have done it and it's stable, then sign me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the union should be at the table. Have you ever been involved yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a member, I go to meetings when I'm not on nights, but I've never been a delegate. If they start pulling trucks off the road, I'll probably have to stop just paying my dues and actually turn up.

S1.say: He'd say the company needs a proper, paid plan for workers who lose their seats, especially truck drivers, and the union should be at the table from day one.
S1.think: He thinks his shovel job lasts longer than the trucks because loading a changing face is harder to automate, but losing the trucks means losing half his friends at work.
S1.do: Asks to train on the remote operating station once it's proven on site and brings two younger operators with him. Learns the autonomous haulage software properly, saves a few hundred extra a month, and gets more active in the union.
S1.feel: Uneasy, and guilty about probably being fine when others aren't.
S1.quote: If they start pulling trucks off the road, I'll probably have to stop just paying my dues and actually turn up.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal's steadiness shows in his timing: he'd move into the remote room, but only after it's proven. His progressive views show up as concern for drivers and a sense he should become active in the union. The guilt of being among the winners is a real thread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need government involved. Something this big can't be left to the mining companies and the tech companies to sort out between them. I'd be pushing for an income guarantee and saying it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my seat goes too. The shovel, the remote room, the supervisor job, the lot. Two years is barely enough time to finish the supervisor course, never mind pick a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop the house plans and keep the money where I can reach it. I'd go to every union meeting and push for long notice periods and big redundancy payouts, and I'd vote and campaign for whoever backs an income guarantee. I wouldn't sign up for any course in the first few months, because I wouldn't know what to train for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That sick feeling, like when the shovel's tracks slip on a wet ramp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or plan goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The house, definitely. We'd keep renting. We've saved almost a deposit, and in this one I'd rather have that money sitting there than a mortgage and no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad. He was a bus driver for thirty years and he lost the route when they merged the companies. He'd tell me to stay calm and get angry in the right places.

S2.say: He'd say this is exactly why government has to be involved, and that a change this big can't be left to mining and tech companies. He'd push for an income guarantee everywhere.
S2.think: He thinks his whole path goes too: the shovel, the remote room and the supervisor job. Two years is too short to change careers.
S2.do: Stops the house plans and keeps savings accessible. Goes to every union meeting pushing for long notice and big redundancy payouts, and votes and campaigns for an income guarantee, holding off on any course until it's clear what to train for.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with a sick, slipping feeling.
S2.quote: We've saved almost a deposit, and in this one I'd rather have that money sitting there than a mortgage and no job.
S2.fieldNote: His steady, wait-until-proven style leaves him with no move to make in two years, which is what turns him alarmed. He turns to collective and political answers, consistent with his views. He leans on his father, who lost a job to a company merger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so use it. Governments should fund training now and companies should be made to keep people on through the change. I'd say it calmly, which I think would land better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can still be useful for most of it. Somebody has to run the machines while the robots are being tested. But I'd still be out by thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a certificate in mechatronics, that's mechanical and electrical systems together, at night school, because someone will be maintaining these machines for a while. I'd be a union delegate by then. I'd save hard, maybe a third of every pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan. That helps more than I'd have guessed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you train for, with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something that keeps me near the machines but not in the seat. Maintenance, commissioning, maybe training robot systems on site. Robots have to learn a pit, and I know this pit better than any engineer from head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change how you think about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy smaller, maybe a two-bedroom unit instead of the house with a yard. Or we'd wait two years and see how it's moving. Ines would want to decide together, so it's not just mine to call.

S3.say: He'd say five years is a warning to use: governments should fund training now and companies should keep people on through the change.
S3.think: He thinks he can stay useful for most of the five years while robots are tested, but still expects to be out of work by 32.
S3.do: Starts a mechatronics certificate at night school in the first year, becomes a union delegate, and saves around a third of each pay. Considers a smaller home or waiting two years before buying.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, because he has a plan.
S3.quote: Robots have to learn a pit, and I know this pit better than any engineer from head office.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Jamal a proven path to follow, which suits his style. He imagines turning his local knowledge of the pit into a role teaching or maintaining robots. The house decision becomes something to shrink rather than cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if we start now and nobody can say they weren't told. I'd want the union and the government building the plan together, starting this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is most of my thirties. I'd get to buy the house, be a supervisor, maybe do the move into maintenance properly. It still ends in the same place, but I'd be older and have more saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house in a couple of years as planned. I'd do the supervisor course first, then the mechatronics certificate, and move into maintenance planning around year four or five. I'd become a delegate and push for a ten-year transition agreement at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's in the background but it's not stopping me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between the five-year and the ten-year one for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five I'm rushing. With ten I get to do it in the right order, like a normal career, just with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the mine you'd try to bring along?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Andile, he's twenty-two and he's one of the best young truck drivers I've ever seen. I'd want him in the training with me. The young ones have the most years of being out of work ahead of them.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty if work starts now, and he'd want the union and government to build the plan together this year.
S4.think: He thinks he'd get most of his thirties: the house, a supervisor role and a proper move into maintenance, before ending up at the same place with more saved.
S4.do: Buys the house in a couple of years as planned and takes the supervisor course, then the mechatronics certificate, moving into maintenance planning around year four or five. Becomes a delegate and pushes for a ten-year transition agreement.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but the worry stays in the background.
S4.quote: With ten I get to do it in the right order, like a normal career, just with a deadline.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Jamal's careful style work for him, which is why he calms down. He'd still bring others along, naming a young driver he wants trained with him. The end point hasn't changed for him, only the order of things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I don't do well with no time to look before I jump. What would help is a guaranteed income for a few years while people retrain, and the company having to pay into it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to the town. Every café and garage in our town lives off miners' pay packets. If we go, the barista goes too. Nobody seems to count them.

headlineQuote: Every café and garage in our town lives off miners' pay packets. If we go, the barista goes too.
portrait: Jamal Rossi is a 27-year-old lead operator on an electric rope shovel at a large open-pit copper mine, training newer operators and living with his partner Ines. He has strong savings, a share account and a plan to buy a home, and he uses AI tools now and then to translate safety notes for a mixed crew. He moves once things are proven, which keeps him calm in the mild pictures and alarmed when AGI comes in two years with no time to watch others go first. With five or ten years he plans night-school mechatronics and a move into maintenance, while becoming more active in the union and backing an income guarantee.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he doesn't do well without time to look before he jumps.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for a few years while people retrain, with companies required to pay into it.
